# Opening position can signal a human reader's theme; proportion remains conjectural

An intelligible opening claim gives a human reader an early cue to what a document is about. This is a reason to move an obscured claim forward, not a guarantee that the reader will remember it. The related idea that supporting material can compete with the claim by occupying disproportionate space is a conjecture. Both ideas concern whether presentation points toward the intended claim, but they have different evidence. LLM judgments can be sensitive to order; the available evidence does not establish the same within-document mechanism for models.

## Position supplies a cue, not a substitute for meaning

In [Kieras's experiments on technical passages](../sources/kieras-initial-mention-as-a-signal-to-thematic-content.ingest.md), readers' immediate main-idea statements resembled the intended theme sentence more closely when it appeared first than when it was embedded in the middle. The proposed explanation is that readers derive the theme largely from meaning, with initial mention guiding that process. Position does not completely determine the theme, and other signals can outweigh it. These were immediate judgments designed to minimize memory demands, not tests of durable recall.

Recall has separate evidence. [Freebody and Anderson's 1981 Technical Report No. 219](../sources/freebody-anderson-serial-position-rated-importance-1981.ingest.md) found that rated importance and serial position independently predicted proposition recall. The overall fitted pattern favored early propositions and, to a lesser extent, late ones. Explained variance was limited, and the pattern was uneven across individual passages. Passage features such as a concluding encapsulation could also contribute. This does not establish a causal chain in which opening placement increases perceived importance and thereby improves recall.

For LLMs, the [position-bias benchmark](../sources/position-bias.ingest.md) compared sibling story edits in both display orders. Judges sometimes changed their underlying preference after the swap. The direction varied by model, including a preference against the first-shown version. This is evidence about comparative writing judgment on those story pairs. It motivates testing order sensitivity in a document-reading task, not assuming that moving a document's claim forward improves an LLM's comprehension or retention.

## Proportion may make support compete with the claim

The conjecture is that space allocated beyond a passage's explanatory role can make its topic seem more central than the claim it supports. A reader might take extended treatment as an importance signal and identify the supporting topic as the document's theme. No position finding above tests this mechanism.

Proportion is relative to what the explanation requires. A short claim may need extensive evidence, qualifications or intermediate reasoning. That support can improve understanding rather than compete with the claim. Its role must therefore be identified independently of the reader's eventual answer: calling everything that precedes a failed answer “disproportionate” would make the conjecture impossible to challenge.

For an LLM, [the argument that context lacks enforced local scope](./llm-context-is-composed-without-scoping.md) supplies a narrower reason to investigate this possibility: labeling material as support does not isolate it from the response. It supplies no law that influence grows with token count. Human use of space as an importance cue and model influence across assigned roles remain different proposed explanations.

A test would compare matched versions with the same intended claim, essential conditions and required support. With claim placement and total length fixed, it would reallocate nonessential elaboration between the claim's explanation and a supporting branch whose role was identified beforehand. The comparison must not strengthen the evidence or remove a needed inference step. Position would be tested separately by moving the claim while preserving content.

The proportion conjecture predicts more substitutions of the supporting topic for the intended claim in the branch-heavy version. No increase, or improved claim identification, would count against that prediction under the tested conditions; the comparison and uncertainty rule must be fixed before observing results. For humans, immediate main-idea selection, later proposition recall and understanding of essential conditions would be separate measures. For LLMs, main-claim extraction or summary would be a specified task, not a durable-memory measure. Reader groups and model configurations would be evaluated separately, with presentation counterbalanced and no exposure to alternative versions. Failure caused by loss of necessary explanation would not establish competition from excess support.

## The repair must address the cause

When placement obscures a claim, moving it addresses placement directly. Shortening elsewhere need not do so. Deleting preceding material can nevertheless help by changing the claim's position or removing competing signals. The rationale favors a cause-specific edit, not brevity for its own sake; it is not a reported experimental comparison of these repairs.

Where support interrupts the reading path, an informative pointer can preserve it elsewhere. This is appropriate only when the claim remains intelligible and its essential conditions stay visible. A pointer changes immediate availability and reading effort, so its benefit needs a separate check: can the reader recover the support when needed and still understand the conditions? A shorter version's success alone would not isolate a proportion effect.

The [compression bundle](../instructions/compression-bundle/README.md) supplies procedures for reviewing placement and the role of supporting material. The rationale here explains why those questions matter without establishing that every flagged passage should be cut.

## Scope

The human placement evidence concerns tested technical passages, not every document genre. Kieras's two-topic main-item materials were explicitly unrepresentative of ordinary prose. The recall findings neither guarantee an opening advantage in each passage nor eliminate late-position advantages. The LLM benchmark used mostly general story situations and measured comparative judgment, not effects of beginning, middle or end placement inside one document.

This note concerns organization inside an opened document. [Claim-bearing titles](./title-as-claim-enables-traversal-as-reasoning.md) instead expose propositions during index scanning and link traversal, before the full note is read. Neither an informative title nor a pointer ensures that a reader follows it. The proposed proportion test remains needed for both human and LLM readers; the cited position studies motivate and bound the rationale rather than corroborate that conjecture.

# Brief: Position and proportion set what a reader retains


## Intent

Explain how text position can influence perceived importance and recall,
for human and LLM readers separately. Present the proposed effect of relative
space allocation as a conjecture, not as an established result of position
studies. The reader should understand
why an intelligible opening claim can guide human theme identification,
why support that outgrows its role might compete with it, and why theme
identification, recall and LLM judgment must remain separate outcomes. Five criteria
currently assume this without stating it: `core-claim-obscured`,
`proportion-mismatch`, `detail-overhang`, `branch-bloat`, and the
surface-the-divergence move in the readability-and-flow pass, together with
the Churchill cue and the operator-brief rule to start with what happens.

## Must keep

- Two readers, two evidence bases. The LLM half may rest on the KB's
  [position-bias ingest](../sources/position-bias.ingest.md) and on
  [LLM context is composed without scoping](./llm-context-is-composed-without-scoping.md);
  the human half needs at least one ingested source on first-mention or
  serial-position effects in text comprehension. Do not let one reader's
  evidence stand for the other's.
- Proportion is relative to explanatory role, not an absolute length or a
  requirement that support be shorter than the claim. Explain the conjecture
  that disproportionate support competes with the claim, name a test, and
  preserve necessary support behind a pointer when that improves the reading
  path without hiding conditions needed to understand the claim.
- The boundary with [title as claim enables traversal as reasoning](./title-as-claim-enables-traversal-as-reasoning.md):
  that note covers position at index level; this note covers position inside
  a document.
- The brevity hazard: shortening alone need not repair a misplaced claim.
  Moving the claim addresses placement directly. Do not imply that deleting
  preceding material can never help; the repair must address the actual cause.

## Must exclude

- A word budget, section budget or any numeric threshold. The compression
  bundle criteria already carry the operational tests.
- A restatement of the compression bundle's four criteria. Link to them as
  the procedures that apply the mechanism.
- Claims about recency or middle-position effects in LLMs beyond what the
  cited ingests support.

## Reserved decisions

- Use Kieras (1980) and Freebody and Anderson's 1981 Technical Report No. 219
  for the human side. Keep one note with distinct human and LLM evidence.
- The operator approved treating proportion as a conjecture with a test;
  no position finding may be presented as a direct test of proportion.
- Do not expand the LLM judgment-order result into a result about retention
  or comprehension within one document.

# Revise an article or note

Make the artifact serve the operator's stated purpose without changing what it
claims, by assessing first and then running only the passes the assessment
recommends.

## Prerequisites

- A purpose in one line: who the reader is and what they should notice or be
  able to do. If the operator named only the artifact, propose the purpose
  at the top of the assessment and proceed under it; the operator corrects
  it if it is wrong.
- The artifact's claims are settled. A claim in dispute goes to the operator
  as a question, not into a pass.

## Steps

1. **Assess before editing.** Read the whole artifact. Report a ranked list
   of changes, highest value against the purpose first, each with its cost
   in one phrase and the pass from this directory that would make it. Name
   the sentence a hostile reviewer would attack first. Say what reads well
   in one sentence. Recommend only passes whose value against the purpose
   is clear; an item you would not defend is not recommended. Do not edit.

   If the highest-value change is a rewrite or a restructuring of the
   argument, report that and stop. The passes work on text, and text a
   rewrite will replace is not worth a pass; recommend passes only over the
   parts the assessment expects to survive.

   Two things the passes cannot own belong in the assessment too. For each
   candidate overclaim, propose whether the sentence is support (may be
   narrowed) or divergence (defend); the divergence items become the
   packets' `Defend:` line unless the operator objects. And list
   qualifications that have gone stale against the body: a scope bullet
   qualifying words the body no longer uses, a table cell filed under the
   wrong row, a cross-note ordinal pointing at the wrong list. These are
   claim questions for the operator, applied as their own commits after
   approval, not passes.

2. **Dispatch each recommended pass as a packet.** Proceed without waiting;
   the report gives the operator the chance to interrupt. Run passes one at a time,
   since they share one write scope. Order them by depth, not by the
   assessment's ranking: a pass whose edits a later pass would rewrite runs
   after it. The order that has held is split-out-a-treatment,
   narrow-overclaims, abstractions, readability-and-flow, plain-wording,
   opening-and-title. Abstractions runs before the structural moves although
   it is a wording pass, because one name per thing is what makes a
   duplicated caveat or two paragraphs on one subject visible; the opening
   runs last because the TL;DR restates a body the earlier passes have
   settled. Make the plain-wording list after the structural moves land; a
   list made against the earlier text names passages that have moved or
   gone. Each pass file carries an `effort`
   field: `simple` passes run in a fresh worker on a cheaper model or lower
   effort; `judgment` passes run on the session model, in the current
   context or a fresh worker. Use a fresh worker when the pass benefits from
   not having seen the conversation, as the plain-wording and
   readability passes do; run narrow-overclaims in the parent context, where
   the conversation is the evidence. Apply one-word swaps and two-sentence
   narrowings in the parent context rather than as packets. Small scoped
   edits from different passes may share one packet when its scope is
   enumerated. The packet is:

   ```
   Purpose: {the operator's one line}
   Artifact: {path}
   Pass: {absolute path of {pass}.md in this instruction's directory}
   Defend: {claims the operator has marked as divergence; a pass may not narrow them}
   Write scope: {the artifact only | none, return proposals}
   Return: the pass's report, plus items noticed but not applied, nothing committed
   ```

   The worker chooses means within the pass. It does not widen the write
   scope, add claims, or remove evidence.

3. **Integrate.** After each pass read the diff, and read every replaced
   phrase in its full sentence, not in the diff summary; a literal
   replacement can supply a referent the original left implicit and supply
   the wrong one. List each mapping, contrast, example, price, or link the
   diff removed and check that the pass report accounts for it; restore what
   it does not, in the classes [audit-a-prior-pass](./audit-a-prior-pass.md)
   uses. A pass that narrows or tightens a sentence tends to take its
   neighbours with it. Run `commonplace-validate` on the artifact, and commit the
   pass alone with a body saying what it was meant to make true. If the operator reverts part of a pass, record the
   threshold they applied in the pass file or a memory, so the next run
   starts from it.

4. **Stop when the recommended passes are done.** Report what each pass
   changed. Items you assessed but did not recommend, and the not-applied
   items the workers returned, are listed once, not run.

## Run it as a workflow

`commonplace-review run revise ARTIFACT --purpose TEXT [--defend CLAIM ...]`
runs these steps with headless workers, which never write the checkout. Its
run directory is derived from the artifact's path and the hash of its text.
It stops with a proposal wherever this procedure waits for the operator.
Repeating alone never approves the proposal or starts its dependent work.
A repeat reuses the recorded `--purpose`, `--defend` and profiles unless you
give them again. Each approval stop prints a JSON report whose `waiting-for` gives
what to do, the file, proposal key, `approve-command` and command to repeat.
Assessment, planning and settled intermediate passes are preauthorized;
never wait for routine plan approval. Selection proposals may be edited
before their `approve-command`; final publication manifests must remain
exactly as generated. Then repeat the workflow command. Approval captures
that text; later selection edits require approval again and are listed under
`unapproved-edits`. Changed proposal inputs require fresh approval. An agent
may approve only on the operator's stated word for that specific proposal;
it must not infer approval from a request to retry. This instruction and the
pass files own judgment; worker prompts name inputs, not additional criteria.

1. Step 1 runs as one assessment ask, on the profile for `judgment`. The run
   retains `assessment.md` and `plan.yaml` under the run directory's
   `artifact/` for inspection and proceeds with the validated plan.
   `--plan FILE` supplies an explicit input or override without assessment
   or approval, including replacement of a stopped plan. The plan holds
   `purpose`, `defend`, `passes` in run order (each a `pass` name and an
   optional `scope`) and `stop`. A plan with `stop` set ends the run without
   editing the artifact. To run passes instead, supply a replacement with
   `stop` cleared and the desired passes through `--plan`; editing the
   retained `artifact/plan.yaml` alone is not an override.
   The command rejects a plan that names an unknown pass, misses a field or
   breaks the depth order the pass files declare. A replacement supplied
   with `--plan` reuses calls whose inputs did not change and reruns the others.
2. Step 2 runs each listed pass as one worker, on the profile from
   `instructions/review-profiles.yaml` that its `effort` selects. Code checks
   the revised text (title, type, brief declaration and H1 kept; no new validation
   failure), and the next pass works on that text. Every pass must end
   `applied`, `no-change` or `skipped` before final publication is offered.
   After a `problem` pass, or while the run waits, the original artifact is
   untouched, and `not-applied` names the run file holding the proposed text.
   The workflow does not commit.
3. Plain-wording and abstractions stop with `artifact/<pass>-list-<key>.md`.
   Delete each entry you strike, with its indented lines, run the stop's
   approval command, then repeat; the worker applies only the approved entries. A list made again for
   another text gets a new file and stops again. These are temporary
   procedure-development points for unsettled selection rules. Retain the
   proposed, accepted and rejected choices with their reasons. Use them to
   revise selection rules and checks, then evaluate those changes on retained
   and fresh examples before seeking separate authorization to remove a
   selection stop. This requires no new automatic learning infrastructure;
   fewer proposals alone do not establish reliability.
4. Narrow-overclaims runs only when the plan's `defend` list is not empty.
   Split-out-a-treatment does not run. Both are reported as skipped, left
   for this procedure in a conversation.
5. For a changed final artifact, inspect `artifact/final.md` and
   `artifact/final.diff`, then approve the exact generated
   `artifact/publication.json` using the report's
   `commonplace-review approve RUN FILE --key KEY` command. Repeat to
   publish. The command writes the original once, only after this approval
   and only if the original and captured brief are unchanged. Repeating
   never approves. Do not edit the manifest or candidate to revise the text:
   supply `--plan`, change workflow inputs, or start a new run. An edited
   manifest cannot authorize publication; the generated manifest must match
   the captured approval exactly.
6. An artifact edited between invocations has another hash, so the command
   opens a new run and assesses again; `--plan FILE` names a plan and skips
   the assessment. An artifact changed during a run is a conflict: nothing
   is written, and the report names the run file holding the proposed text.

Step 3 stays with the operator: each pass's report and the text it left are
under `artifact/reports/` and `artifact/texts/`; read each diff before final
approval. If a report does not account for an edit, revise through workflow
inputs or `--plan`, not by editing the generated candidate. Commit only after
approved publication. Use this procedure in a
conversation instead when the passes are chosen as the conversation goes,
when a pass needs the conversation as evidence, or when each pass should be
integrated and committed before the next one runs.

## Headless write briefs

When the artifact declares a [write brief](../../types/write-brief.md), the assessment and every pass
(including candidate-list and apply workers) receive its captured text as
`brief`. Pass workers also receive this revision instruction as `workflow`;
apply its constraints to the assigned pass, not additional passes or the
interactive dispatch procedure.

Treat the supplied brief as binding retained intent. Keep its must-keep,
must-exclude and reserved decisions in both the plan and the edited text.
Do not amend the brief or remove or change the artifact's `brief:` field.
If the purpose, defended claims, validated plan, approved candidate list or
pass instruction conflicts with it, report the conflict through the
worker-problem output and stop. Selection or publication approval does not authorise
amending the brief. The operator must resolve the commission change outside
this workflow before continuing.

Use the captured input, not a reread of the live brief. A brief change between
invocations invalidates affected calls and dependent approvals; a change during an
invocation blocks publication. A missing or invalid declared brief stops the
run before workers launch. Supplying it does not mechanically verify that
an edit respects its meaning; the worker must identify conflicts.

## Budget

- The assessment is one full read. Each pass is one more. Do not re-read
  linked notes unless a pass names them.
- A worker gets the artifact path and the packet, never the conversation.
- Propose-only work (the assessment, the plain-wording list, title
  proposals) may run in parallel; edits to the artifact run in sequence.
- Stop when the recommended passes are done. An item not recommended costs
  nothing; recommending a pass of unclear value costs a read and a diff.

## Verify

- Every applied change traces to a recommended pass.
- Every passage a diff weakened is accounted for by that pass's report.
- No claim, evidence, or qualification changed unless the operator asked.
- Conversational execution validates and commits each integrated pass. The
  headless workflow instead retains per-pass reports and checked texts, then
  permits one final write only after publication approval.
- Operator reverts have been recorded as thresholds.

## Proportion may make support compete with the claim

The conjecture is that space allocated beyond a passage's explanatory role can make its topic seem more central than the claim it supports. A reader might take extended treatment as an importance signal and identify the supporting topic as the document's theme. No position finding above tests this mechanism.

Proportion is relative to what the explanation requires. A short claim may need extensive evidence, qualifications or intermediate reasoning. That support can improve understanding rather than compete with the claim. Its role must therefore be identified independently of the reader's eventual answer: calling everything that precedes a failed answer “disproportionate” would make the conjecture impossible to challenge.

For an LLM, [the argument that context lacks enforced local scope](./llm-context-is-composed-without-scoping.md) supplies a narrower reason to investigate this possibility: labeling material as support does not isolate it from the response. It supplies no law that influence grows with token count. Human use of space as an importance cue and model influence across assigned roles remain different proposed explanations.

A test would compare matched versions with the same intended claim, essential conditions and required support. With claim placement and total length fixed, it would reallocate nonessential elaboration between the claim's explanation and a supporting branch whose role was identified beforehand. The comparison must not strengthen the evidence or remove a needed inference step. Position would be tested separately by moving the claim while preserving content.

The proportion conjecture predicts more substitutions of the supporting topic for the intended claim in the branch-heavy version. No increase, or improved claim identification, would count against that prediction under the tested conditions; the comparison and uncertainty rule must be fixed before observing results. For humans, immediate main-idea selection, later proposition recall and understanding of essential conditions would be separate measures. For LLMs, main-claim extraction or summary would be a specified task, not a durable-memory measure. Reader groups and model configurations would be evaluated separately, with presentation counterbalanced and no exposure to alternative versions. Failure caused by loss of necessary explanation would not establish competition from excess support.

## The repair must address the cause

When placement obscures a claim, moving it addresses placement directly. Shortening elsewhere need not do so. Deleting preceding material can nevertheless help by changing the claim's position or removing competing signals. The rationale favors a cause-specific edit, not brevity for its own sake; it is not a reported experimental comparison of these repairs.

Where support interrupts the reading path, an informative pointer can preserve it elsewhere. This is appropriate only when the claim remains intelligible and its essential conditions stay visible. A pointer changes immediate availability and reading effort, so its benefit needs a separate check: can the reader recover the support when needed and still understand the conditions? A shorter version's success alone would not isolate a proportion effect.

The [compression bundle](../instructions/compression-bundle/README.md) supplies procedures for reviewing placement and the role of supporting material. The rationale here explains why those questions matter without establishing that every flagged passage should be cut.

## Scope

The human placement evidence concerns tested technical passages, not every document genre. Kieras's two-topic main-item materials were explicitly unrepresentative of ordinary prose. The recall findings neither guarantee an opening advantage in each passage nor eliminate late-position advantages. The LLM benchmark used mostly general story situations and measured comparative judgment, not effects of beginning, middle or end placement inside one document.

This note concerns organization inside an opened document. [Claim-bearing titles](./title-as-claim-enables-traversal-as-reasoning.md) instead expose propositions during index scanning and link traversal, before the full note is read. Neither an informative title nor a pointer ensures that a reader follows it. The proposed proportion test remains needed for both human and LLM readers; the cited position studies motivate and bound the rationale rather than corroborate that conjecture.

# Revise an article or note

Make the artifact serve the operator's stated purpose without changing what it
claims, by assessing first and then running only the passes the assessment
recommends.

## Prerequisites

- A purpose in one line: who the reader is and what they should notice or be
  able to do. If the operator named only the artifact, propose the purpose
  at the top of the assessment and proceed under it; the operator corrects
  it if it is wrong.
- The artifact's claims are settled. A claim in dispute goes to the operator
  as a question, not into a pass.

## Steps

1. **Assess before editing.** Read the whole artifact. Report a ranked list
   of changes, highest value against the purpose first, each with its cost
   in one phrase and the pass from this directory that would make it. Name
   the sentence a hostile reviewer would attack first. Say what reads well
   in one sentence. Recommend only passes whose value against the purpose
   is clear; an item you would not defend is not recommended. Do not edit.

   If the highest-value change is a rewrite or a restructuring of the
   argument, report that and stop. The passes work on text, and text a
   rewrite will replace is not worth a pass; recommend passes only over the
   parts the assessment expects to survive.

   Two things the passes cannot own belong in the assessment too. For each
   candidate overclaim, propose whether the sentence is support (may be
   narrowed) or divergence (defend); the divergence items become the
   packets' `Defend:` line unless the operator objects. And list
   qualifications that have gone stale against the body: a scope bullet
   qualifying words the body no longer uses, a table cell filed under the
   wrong row, a cross-note ordinal pointing at the wrong list. These are
   claim questions for the operator, applied as their own commits after
   approval, not passes.

2. **Dispatch each recommended pass as a packet.** Proceed without waiting;
   the report gives the operator the chance to interrupt. Run passes one at a time,
   since they share one write scope. Order them by depth, not by the
   assessment's ranking: a pass whose edits a later pass would rewrite runs
   after it. The order that has held is split-out-a-treatment,
   narrow-overclaims, abstractions, readability-and-flow, plain-wording,
   opening-and-title. Abstractions runs before the structural moves although
   it is a wording pass, because one name per thing is what makes a
   duplicated caveat or two paragraphs on one subject visible; the opening
   runs last because the TL;DR restates a body the earlier passes have
   settled. Make the plain-wording list after the structural moves land; a
   list made against the earlier text names passages that have moved or
   gone. Each pass file carries an `effort`

   effort; `judgment` passes run on the session model, in the current
   context or a fresh worker. Use a fresh worker when the pass benefits from
   not having seen the conversation, as the plain-wording and
   readability passes do; run narrow-overclaims in the parent context, where
   the conversation is the evidence. Apply one-word swaps and two-sentence

   Purpose: {the operator's one line}
   Artifact: {path}
   Pass: {absolute path of {pass}.md in this instruction's directory}
   Defend: {claims the operator has marked as divergence; a pass may not narrow them}
   Write scope: {the artifact only | none, return proposals}
   Return: the pass's report, plus items noticed but not applied, nothing committed

   neighbours with it. Run `commonplace-validate` on the artifact, and commit the

   threshold they applied in the pass file or a memory, so the next run
   starts from it.

   changed. Items you assessed but did not recommend, and the not-applied
   items the workers returned, are listed once, not run.

`commonplace-review run revise ARTIFACT --purpose TEXT [--defend CLAIM ...]`

run directory is derived from the artifact's path and the hash of its text.

conversation instead when the passes are chosen as the conversation goes,
when a pass needs the conversation as evidence, or when each pass should be
integrated and committed before the next one runs.

When the artifact declares a [write brief](../../types/write-brief.md), the assessment and every pass
(including candidate-list and apply workers) receive its captured text as
`brief`. Pass workers also receive this revision instruction as `workflow`;

interactive dispatch procedure.

- The assessment is one full read. Each pass is one more. Do not re-read
  linked notes unless a pass names them.
- A worker gets the artifact path and the packet, never the conversation.
- Propose-only work (the assessment, the plain-wording list, title

- Every applied change traces to a recommended pass.
- Every passage a diff weakened is accounted for by that pass's report.
- No claim, evidence, or qualification changed unless the operator asked.
- Each pass has its own commit and validation passed before it.
- Operator reverts have been recorded as thresholds.

# Opening position can signal a human reader's theme; proportion remains conjectural

An intelligible opening claim gives a human reader an early cue to what a document is about. This is a reason to move an obscured claim forward, not a guarantee that the reader will remember it. The related idea that supporting material can compete with the claim by occupying disproportionate space is a conjecture. Both ideas concern whether presentation points toward the intended claim, but they have different evidence. LLM judgments can be sensitive to order; the available evidence does not establish the same within-document mechanism for models.

## Position supplies a cue, not a substitute for meaning

In [Kieras's experiments on technical passages](../sources/kieras-initial-mention-as-a-signal-to-thematic-content.ingest.md), readers' immediate main-idea statements resembled the intended theme sentence more closely when it appeared first than when it was embedded in the middle. The proposed explanation is that readers derive the theme largely from meaning, with initial mention guiding that process. Position does not completely determine the theme, and other signals can outweigh it. These were immediate judgments designed to minimize memory demands, not tests of durable recall.

Recall has separate evidence. [Freebody and Anderson's 1981 Technical Report No. 219](../sources/freebody-anderson-serial-position-rated-importance-1981.ingest.md) found that rated importance and serial position independently predicted proposition recall. The overall fitted pattern favored early propositions and, to a lesser extent, late ones. Explained variance was limited, and the pattern was uneven across individual passages. Passage features such as a concluding encapsulation could also contribute. This does not establish a causal chain in which opening placement increases perceived importance and thereby improves recall.

For LLMs, the [position-bias benchmark](../sources/position-bias.ingest.md) compared sibling story edits in both display orders. Judges sometimes changed their underlying preference after the swap. The direction varied by model, including a preference against the first-shown version. This is evidence about comparative writing judgment on those story pairs. It motivates testing order sensitivity in a document-reading task, not assuming that moving a document's claim forward improves an LLM's comprehension or retention.

## Proportion may make support compete with the claim

The conjecture is that space allocated beyond a passage's explanatory role can make its topic seem more central than the claim it supports. A reader might take extended treatment as an importance signal and identify the supporting topic as the document's theme. No position finding above tests this mechanism.

Proportion is relative to what the explanation requires. A short claim may need extensive evidence, qualifications or intermediate reasoning. That support can improve understanding rather than compete with the claim. Its role must therefore be identified independently of the reader's eventual answer: calling everything that precedes a failed answer “disproportionate” would make the conjecture impossible to challenge.

For an LLM, [the argument that context lacks enforced local scope](./llm-context-is-composed-without-scoping.md) supplies a narrower reason to investigate this possibility: labeling material as support does not isolate it from the response. It supplies no law that influence grows with token count. Human use of space as an importance cue and model influence across assigned roles remain different proposed explanations.

A test would compare matched versions with the same intended claim, essential conditions and required support. With claim placement and total length fixed, it would reallocate nonessential elaboration between the claim's explanation and a supporting branch whose role was identified beforehand. The comparison must not strengthen the evidence or remove a needed inference step. Position would be tested separately by moving the claim while preserving content.

The proportion conjecture predicts more substitutions of the supporting topic for the intended claim in the branch-heavy version. No increase, or improved claim identification, would count against that prediction under the tested conditions; the comparison and uncertainty rule must be fixed before observing results. For humans, immediate main-idea selection, later proposition recall and understanding of essential conditions would be separate measures. For LLMs, main-claim extraction or summary would be a specified task, not a durable-memory measure. Reader groups and model configurations would be evaluated separately, with presentation counterbalanced and no exposure to alternative versions. Failure caused by loss of necessary explanation would not establish competition from excess support.

## The repair must address the cause

When placement obscures a claim, moving it addresses placement directly. Shortening elsewhere need not do so. Deleting preceding material can nevertheless help by changing the claim's position or removing competing signals. The rationale favors a cause-specific edit, not brevity for its own sake; it is not a reported experimental comparison of these repairs.

Where support interrupts the reading path, an informative pointer can preserve it elsewhere. This is appropriate only when the claim remains intelligible and its essential conditions stay visible. A pointer changes immediate availability and reading effort, so its benefit needs a separate check: can the reader recover the support when needed and still understand the conditions? A shorter version's success alone would not isolate a proportion effect.

The [compression bundle](../instructions/compression-bundle/README.md) supplies procedures for reviewing placement and the role of supporting material. The rationale here explains why those questions matter without establishing that every flagged passage should be cut.

## Scope

The recall findings neither guarantee an opening advantage in each passage nor eliminate late-position advantages. The LLM benchmark used mostly general story situations and measured comparative judgment, not effects of beginning, middle or end placement inside one document.

# Revise an article or note

Make the artifact serve the operator's stated purpose without changing what it
claims, by assessing first and then running only the passes the assessment
recommends.

## Prerequisites

- A purpose in one line: who the reader is and what they should notice or be
  able to do. If the operator named only the artifact, propose the purpose
  at the top of the assessment and proceed under it; the operator corrects
  it if it is wrong.
- The artifact's claims are settled. A claim in dispute goes to the operator
  as a question, not into a pass.

## Steps

1. **Assess before editing.** Read the whole artifact. Report a ranked list
   of changes, highest value against the purpose first, each with its cost
   in one phrase and the pass from this directory that would make it. Name
   the sentence a hostile reviewer would attack first. Say what reads well
   in one sentence. Recommend only passes whose value against the purpose
   is clear; an item you would not defend is not recommended. Do not edit.

   If the highest-value change is a rewrite or a restructuring of the
   argument, report that and stop. The passes work on text, and text a
   rewrite will replace is not worth a pass; recommend passes only over the
   parts the assessment expects to survive.

   Two things the passes cannot own belong in the assessment too. For each
   candidate overclaim, propose whether the sentence is support (may be
   narrowed) or divergence (defend); the divergence items become the
   packets' `Defend:` line unless the operator objects. And list
   qualifications that have gone stale against the body: a scope bullet
   qualifying words the body no longer uses, a table cell filed under the
   wrong row, a cross-note ordinal pointing at the wrong list. These are
   claim questions for the operator, applied as their own commits after
   approval, not passes.

2. **Dispatch each recommended pass as a packet.** Proceed without waiting;
   the report gives the operator the chance to interrupt. Run passes one at a time,
   since they share one write scope. Order them by depth, not by the
   assessment's ranking: a pass whose edits a later pass would rewrite runs
   after it. The order that has held is split-out-a-treatment,
   narrow-overclaims, abstractions, readability-and-flow, plain-wording,
   opening-and-title. Abstractions runs before the structural moves although
   it is a wording pass, because one name per thing is what makes a
   duplicated caveat or two paragraphs on one subject visible; the opening
   runs last because the TL;DR restates a body the earlier passes have
   settled. Make the plain-wording list after the structural moves land; a
   list made against the earlier text names passages that have moved or
   gone. Each pass file carries an `effort`
   field: `simple` passes run in a fresh worker on a cheaper model or lower
   effort; `judgment` passes run on the session model, in the current
   context or a fresh worker. Use a fresh worker when the pass benefits from
   not having seen the conversation, as the plain-wording and
   readability passes do; run narrow-overclaims in the parent context, where
   the conversation is the evidence. Apply one-word swaps and two-sentence
   narrowings in the parent context rather than as packets. Small scoped
   edits from different passes may share one packet when its scope is
   enumerated. The packet is:

   ```
   Purpose: {the operator's one line}
   Artifact: {path}
   Pass: {absolute path of {pass}.md in this instruction's directory}
   Defend: {claims the operator has marked as divergence; a pass may not narrow them}
   Write scope: {the artifact only | none, return proposals}
   Return: the pass's report, plus items noticed but not applied, nothing committed
   ```

   The worker chooses means within the pass. It does not widen the write
   scope, add claims, or remove evidence.

3. **Integrate.** After each pass read the diff, and read every replaced
   phrase in its full sentence, not in the diff summary; a literal
   replacement can supply a referent the original left implicit and supply
   the wrong one. List each mapping, contrast, example, price, or link the
   diff removed and check that the pass report accounts for it; restore what
   it does not, in the classes [audit-a-prior-pass](./audit-a-prior-pass.md)
   uses. A pass that narrows or tightens a sentence tends to take its
   neighbours with it. Run `commonplace-validate` on the artifact, and commit the
   pass alone with a body saying what it was meant to make true. If the operator reverts part of a pass, record the
   threshold they applied in the pass file or a memory, so the next run
   starts from it.

4. **Stop when the recommended passes are done.** Report what each pass
   changed. Items you assessed but did not recommend, and the not-applied
   items the workers returned, are listed once, not run.

## Run it as a workflow

`commonplace-review run revise ARTIFACT --purpose TEXT [--defend CLAIM ...]`
runs these steps with headless workers, which never write the checkout. Its
run directory is derived from the artifact's path and the hash of its text.
It stops with a proposal wherever this procedure waits for the operator.
Repeating alone never approves the proposal or starts its dependent work.
A repeat reuses the recorded `--purpose`, `--defend` and profiles unless you
give them again. Each approval stop prints a JSON report whose `waiting-for` gives
what to do, the file, proposal key, `approve-command` and command to repeat.
Assessment, planning and settled intermediate passes are preauthorized;
never wait for routine plan approval. Selection proposals may be edited
before their `approve-command`; final publication manifests must remain
exactly as generated. Then repeat the workflow command. Approval captures
that text; later selection edits require approval again and are listed under
`unapproved-edits`. Changed proposal inputs require fresh approval. An agent
may approve only on the operator's stated word for that specific proposal;
it must not infer approval from a request to retry. This instruction and the
pass files own judgment; worker prompts name inputs, not additional criteria.

1. Step 1 runs as one assessment ask, on the profile for `judgment`. The run
   retains `assessment.md` and `plan.yaml` under the run directory's
   `artifact/` for inspection and proceeds with the validated plan.
   `--plan FILE` supplies an explicit input or override without assessment
   or approval, including replacement of a stopped plan. The plan holds
   `purpose`, `defend`, `passes` in run order (each a `pass` name and an
   optional `scope`) and `stop`. A plan with `stop` set ends the run without
   editing the artifact. To run passes instead, supply a replacement with
   `stop` cleared and the desired passes through `--plan`; editing the
   retained `artifact/plan.yaml` alone is not an override.

   breaks the depth order the pass files declare. A replacement supplied
   with `--plan` reuses calls whose inputs did not change and reruns the others.

   `applied`, `no-change` or `skipped` before final publication is offered.

   untouched, and `not-applied` names the run file holding the proposed text.

3. Plain-wording and abstractions stop with `artifact/<pass>-list-<key>.md`.

4. Narrow-overclaims runs only when the plan's `defend` list is not empty.

5. For a changed final artifact, inspect `artifact/final.md` and

   `artifact/publication.json` using the report's
   `commonplace-review approve RUN FILE --key KEY` command. Repeat to

   and only if the original and captured brief are unchanged. Repeating
   never approves. Do not edit the manifest or candidate to revise the text:
   supply `--plan`, change workflow inputs, or start a new run. An edited
   manifest cannot authorize publication; the generated manifest must match
   the captured approval exactly.
6. An artifact edited between invocations has another hash, so the command
   opens a new run and assesses again; `--plan FILE` names a plan and skips
   the assessment. An artifact changed during a run is a conflict: nothing
   is written, and the report names the run file holding the proposed text.

Step 3 stays with the operator: each pass's report and the text it left are
under `artifact/reports/` and `artifact/texts/`; read each diff before final
approval. If a report does not account for an edit, revise through workflow
inputs or `--plan`, not by editing the generated candidate. Commit only after
approved publication. Use this procedure in a
conversation instead when the passes are chosen as the conversation goes,
when a pass needs the conversation as evidence, or when each pass should be
integrated and committed before the next one runs.

## Headless write briefs

When the artifact declares a [write brief](../../types/write-brief.md), the assessment and every pass
(including candidate-list and apply workers) receive its captured text as

must-exclude and reserved decisions in both the plan and the edited text.
Do not amend the brief or remove or change the artifact's `brief:` field.

- The assessment is one full read. Each pass is one more. Do not re-read
  linked notes unless a pass names them.
- A worker gets the artifact path and the packet, never the conversation.
- Propose-only work (the assessment, the plain-wording list, title

- Every passage a diff weakened is accounted for by that pass's report.
- No claim, evidence, or qualification changed unless the operator asked.
- Conversational execution validates and commits each integrated pass. The

# Opening position can signal a human reader's theme; proportion remains conjectural

An intelligible opening claim gives a human reader an early cue to what a document is about. This is a reason to move an obscured claim forward, not a guarantee that the reader will remember it. The related idea that supporting material can compete with the claim by occupying disproportionate space is a conjecture. Both ideas concern whether presentation points toward the intended claim, but they have different evidence. LLM judgments can be sensitive to order; the available evidence does not establish the same within-document mechanism for models.

## Position supplies a cue, not a substitute for meaning

In [Kieras's experiments on technical passages](../sources/kieras-initial-mention-as-a-signal-to-thematic-content.ingest.md), readers' immediate main-idea statements resembled the intended theme sentence more closely when it appeared first than when it was embedded in the middle. The proposed explanation is that readers derive the theme largely from meaning, with initial mention guiding that process. Position does not completely determine the theme, and other signals can outweigh it. These were immediate judgments designed to minimize memory demands, not tests of durable recall. The findings concern the tested technical passages, not every document genre. Kieras’s two-topic main-item materials were explicitly unrepresentative of ordinary prose.

Recall has separate evidence. [Freebody and Anderson's 1981 Technical Report No. 219](../sources/freebody-anderson-serial-position-rated-importance-1981.ingest.md) found that rated importance and serial position independently predicted proposition recall. The overall fitted pattern favored early propositions and, to a lesser extent, late ones. Explained variance was limited, and the pattern was uneven across individual passages: the findings neither guarantee an opening advantage in each passage nor eliminate late-position advantages. Passage features such as a concluding encapsulation could also contribute. This does not establish a causal chain in which opening placement increases perceived importance and thereby improves recall.

For LLMs, the [position-bias benchmark](../sources/position-bias.ingest.md) compared sibling story edits in both display orders. Judges sometimes changed their underlying preference after the swap. The direction varied by model, including a preference against the first-shown version. This is evidence about comparative writing judgment on those story pairs, which used mostly general story situations. The benchmark did not measure the effects of beginning, middle or end placement inside one document. It motivates testing order sensitivity in a document-reading task, not assuming that moving a document's claim forward improves an LLM's comprehension or retention.

## Proportion may make support compete with the claim

The conjecture is that space allocated beyond a passage's explanatory role can make its topic seem more central than the claim it supports. A reader might take extended treatment as an importance signal and identify the supporting topic as the document's theme. No position finding above tests this mechanism.

Proportion is relative to what the explanation requires. A short claim may need extensive evidence, qualifications or intermediate reasoning. That support can improve understanding rather than compete with the claim. Its role must therefore be identified independently of the reader's eventual answer: calling everything that precedes a failed answer “disproportionate” would make the conjecture impossible to challenge.

For an LLM, [the argument that context lacks enforced local scope](./llm-context-is-composed-without-scoping.md) supplies a narrower reason to investigate this possibility: labeling material as support does not isolate it from the response. It supplies no law that influence grows with token count. Human use of space as an importance cue and model influence across assigned roles remain different proposed explanations.

A test would compare matched versions with the same intended claim, essential conditions and required support. It would keep claim placement and total length fixed while reallocating nonessential elaboration between the claim's explanation and a supporting branch whose role was identified beforehand. The comparison must not strengthen the evidence or remove a needed inference step. Position would be tested separately by moving the claim while preserving content.

The proportion conjecture predicts more substitutions of the supporting topic for the intended claim in the branch-heavy version. No increase, or improved claim identification, would count against that prediction under the tested conditions. The comparison and uncertainty rule must be fixed before observing results. Failure caused by loss of necessary explanation would not establish competition from excess support.

The measures would differ by reader. For humans, the test would measure immediate main-idea selection, later proposition recall and understanding of essential conditions separately. For LLMs, the specified task would be main-claim extraction or summary, not a measure of durable memory. Reader groups and model configurations would be evaluated separately. Presentation would be counterbalanced, and no reader would see alternative versions.

## The repair must address the cause

When placement obscures a claim, moving it addresses placement directly. Shortening elsewhere need not do so. Deleting preceding material can nevertheless help by changing the claim's position or removing competing signals. The rationale favors a cause-specific edit, not brevity for its own sake; it is not a reported experimental comparison of these repairs.

Where support interrupts the reading path, an informative pointer can preserve it elsewhere. This is appropriate only when the claim remains intelligible and its essential conditions stay visible. A pointer changes immediate availability and reading effort, so its benefit needs a separate check: can the reader recover the support when needed and still understand the conditions? A shorter version's success alone would not isolate a proportion effect.

The [compression bundle](../instructions/compression-bundle/README.md) supplies procedures for reviewing placement and the role of supporting material. The rationale here explains why those questions matter without establishing that every flagged passage should be cut.

## Scope

This note concerns organization inside an opened document. [Claim-bearing titles](./title-as-claim-enables-traversal-as-reasoning.md) instead expose propositions during index scanning and link traversal, before the full note is read. Neither an informative title nor a pointer ensures that a reader follows it. The proposed proportion test remains needed for both human and LLM readers; the cited position studies motivate and bound the rationale rather than corroborate that conjecture.
